requests.purpose: Give the film one recognizable robotic arm and sample line that changes state through the film: it takes element vials into a crucible, sets the crucible in a glowing furnace, carries the sample to a test rig, loads and bends the real metal, and at the close tips the melt into a mold, so the planned Aggie AI Foundry action is a drawn object a viewer can follow.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG object in the current Remotion engine. A generic multi-axis robotic arm with a rounded warm gray shell, a visible wrist joint and a two finger gripper holding tongs, no brand marks. Beside it a rack of glass element vials, a ceramic crucible, a furnace opening that glows amber with a heat shimmer, and a sample test rig with a clamp and a needle gauge. Soft key light from the upper left through a lab window, cool fill from the right, contact shadows on a worn steel line bed, scuffed paint and a slightly leaning sample tray so nothing is symmetric. A disclosed illustration of a planned lab, never a real arm, furnace, rig or Texas A&M building.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of a planned automated alloy line. Not an existing Texas A&M facility, not a named arm or furnace model, not a real melting method, and the test shows no measured result.

story_contract.opening_question: How do you find one good alloy among a trillion possible mixes?
story_contract.actor: Texas A&M University Department of Materials Science and Engineering, which announced a $2 million WoodNext Foundation grant
story_contract.action: Announced a grant to build the Aggie AI Foundry, a planned lab where AI proposes alloys and computer-controlled robotic arms mix, melt and test them.
story_contract.change: Alloy development would move toward an automated line where AI proposes and robotic arms make and test the metal, with a goal of a week or less instead of months.
story_contract.affected_people: Materials scientists and students at Texas A&M. No person is named beyond the quoted researcher.
story_contract.consequence: The metal still has to be made and tested, because a computer can predict some behavior but no computer tool can predict an alloy.
story_contract.source_limit: Every verb about the facility is future tense. The release gives no opening date, building, melting method or measured result, and a week or less is the university's goal.
story_contract.closing_answer: The AI can suggest, and only the melt can answer.

captions.text: Several dozen elements can be mixed in roughly a trillion ways.
No person can sort through that many.
Texas A&M announced a two million dollar grant,
to build the Aggie AI Foundry.
The plan is that AI proposes alloys,
and computer-controlled robotic arms mix, melt and test them.
Raymundo Arróyave says a computer can predict some behavior,
but no computer tool anywhere can predict an alloy's behavior.
So the work has to be done on the actual metal.
The goal is developing alloys in a week or less, not months.
That is the university's goal, not a result.
The release gives no opening date.
